newsitem.title: USA: Brawny Brazil a lightweight in New York ADR markets.
newsitem.headline: Brawny Brazil a lightweight in New York ADR markets.

text.p: Brazil, the giant among Latin American economies, is a 98-pound weakling in the surging American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) market but could yet turn into a heavyweight.
While 51 new foreign companies swarmed New York exchanges in the first three quarters of the year, up from 32 in the same period last year, only one of the newcomers was from Brazil.
The country, whose $670 billion economy dwarfs the rest of Latin America, has only three companies with top-drawer trading status as Level 3 ADRs. By comparison, Chile has 19 and Mexico 29.

A Level 3 rating means that the companies being traded conform to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's standards of accounting and reporting, and their shares are as trustworthy as any from a U.S. company.
Analysts and businessmen blame Brazil's own quirks for the marked absence from the busiest financial market in the world.

Many corporations, for example, are family-owned businesses with a lot of cash, a preference for raising money in Sao Paulo, Brazil's financial capital, and ignorance of international markets. So far they have little taste for meeting U.S. accounting standards in exchange for a New York listing.
"Most large Brazilian companies ... are not professionally run," said Agilio Macedo, finance director of Aracruz Celulose SA, the first Brazilian company to be listed on the New York Stock Exchange.
"Most simply don't like to open up their books. It's part of the Brazilian culture -- they are very secretive," he said in a telephone interview from Rio de Janeiro.
Brazilian companies also are just starting to adjust to economic stability and a sound currency as reforms under President Fernando Henrique Cardoso curb decades of high inflation.
Despite the drawbacks Brazil could become an ADR powerhouse as early as next year, helped by the biggest privatisations in Latin American history.
Brazil is drawing up plans to sell off huge state firms probably starting in 1997.

Those expected to be put on the block include Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, the world's biggest producer of iron ore; power firm Eletrobras; and state telephone company Telebras, a Latin American bellwether stock and among the three listed in New York.
Each of those sales is expected to be several times bigger than the 1993 privatisation of Argentine oil company YPF. Its $3 billion sale is the record for Latin American privatisations.
Those sell-offs should prompt more Brazilian companies to jump into the New York market.

Companhia Vale do Rio Doce in particular "will do what YPF did for Argentina and (the sale of state-owned Telefonos de Mexico) did for Mexico. They need one landmark deal," said Greg Bundy, managing director for international equities at Merrill Lynch.
Macedo said he had gotten increasing queries in the last eight to 10 months from other Brazilian companies about listing as a Level 3 ADR.
He forecast a 1997 surge in ADR listings, especially among such recently privatised steel companies as Usiminas and Companhia Siderurgica Nacional and other pulp and paper companies.
"For us it had fantastic results and that is the story I tell whenever I have a chance. When things start moving in Brazil they move very fast," he said.
